# Fact-Check Audit & Revised Report: Creatine Supplementation

**Note on scope:** No draft text was attached to this task, so the audit below covers the complete set of claim clusters that creatine reports typically assert — all of which were verified against the retrieved literature. Each claim is triaged, and the revised report that follows is written with explicit confidence tiers separating established facts from uncertain or disputed material.

---

## Part 1 — Claim-by-Claim Audit

| # | Common draft claim | Verdict | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Creatine improves strength, power, and lean mass with resistance training | **ESTABLISHED** | Meta-analytic and position-stand support [1][36][37] |
| 2 | A loading phase (20–25 g/day × 5–7 days) is **required** | **REJECTED** | Loading only accelerates saturation; 3–5 g/day reaches the same plateau in 3–4 weeks [1][35] |
| 3 | Standard dose is 3–5 g/day creatine monohydrate | **ESTABLISHED** | [1][2] |
| 4 | Early weight gain is "just water bloat" | **MISLEADING AS STATED** | Initial ~1–2 kg is intracellular water; later gains with training are lean mass, not fat [1][36] |
| 5 | Creatine damages the kidneys | **UNSUPPORTED in healthy people** | Biomarker artifact (creatine→creatinine); case reports involved pre-existing renal disease [1][2][5][6][12][13] |
| 6 | Creatine damages the liver | **UNSUPPORTED** | No AST/ALT/ALP/bilirubin changes across trials [1][2][7][8][9] |
| 7 | Creatine causes dehydration and muscle cramps | **UNSUPPORTED / DISPUTED** | Originated as 1998 speculation [23]; refuted by systematic review and trials [18][19][20][21]; one ACSM precaution [22] was theoretical and superseded |
| 8 | Creatine causes hair loss (via DHT) | **DISPUTED — NOT SUPPORTED** | Single 2009 study (n≈20) measured hormones, not hair; DHT stayed within normal range; never replicated [3]; reviews find no evidence [1][2] |
| 9 | Creatine boosts cognition "across the board" | **OVERSTATED** | Pooled effect null in healthy young adults (g ≈ 0.05, ns, 25 RCTs) [25]; benefits are conditional |
| 10 | Creatine improves memory in older adults | **SUPPORTED, MODEST** | g ≈ 0.29–0.32 for memory in ≥65s; evidence quality low-to-moderate [25][28] |
| 11 | Creatine helps cognition during sleep deprivation | **PRELIMINARY** | Two small RCTs only (n≈15–16) [29][30] |
| 12 | Creatine is especially effective in vegetarians | **SUPPORTED, SMALL TRIALS** | [26][31] |
| 13 | Cycling or "receptor downregulation" is needed | **UNSUPPORTED** | [1][2] |
| 14 | Large single doses can cause GI distress | **SUPPORTED** | Dose-related, ≥10 g boluses [24] |
| 15 | Long-term use (up to ~5 years) is safe in healthy adults | **ESTABLISHED** | [1][5][9][10][11] |
| 16 | Creatine is safe in CKD patients, pregnancy, young children | **INSUFFICIENT DATA** | Precaution advised [1][2][16] |

---

## Part 2 — Revised Report

### 1. Efficacy for muscle and performance — **ESTABLISHED**
Creatine monohydrate is one of the most extensively studied supplements in existence. Supplementation reliably increases muscle phosphocreatine stores (~20–40%), improving strength, sprint performance, and lean mass when combined with resistance training [1][36][37]. This should be stated as fact.

### 2. Dosing — **ESTABLISHED, with one common error to correct**
- **Correction required:** A loading phase is *optional*, not necessary. Loading (20–25 g/day split into 4–5 doses for 5–7 days) saturates muscle within ~1 week; 3–5 g/day achieves identical saturation in ~3–4 weeks [1][35]. Excess creatine is excreted.
- 3–5 g/day of **creatine monohydrate** is the evidence-based maintenance dose; larger athletes may need 5–10 g/day [1]. Monohydrate remains the best-studied and most cost-effective form; alternative forms have not demonstrated superiority [1][2]. No cycling is needed [1][2].

### 3. Weight gain — **ESTABLISHED, but drafts often mischaracterize it**
- Phase 1: ~1–2 kg rapid gain in the first week is **intracellular water retention** (osmotic effect), not extracellular bloating [1][2].
- Phase 2: with resistance training, additional gain is **lean mass** (~1–1.5 kg greater fat-free mass vs. placebo), with no increase in fat mass [36][37]. Drafts calling this "water bloat" or implying fat gain should be corrected.

### 4. Kidney and liver safety — **ESTABLISHED for healthy people; state the caveat**
- No consistent evidence of renal or hepatic harm in healthy individuals across short-term trials, long-term observational studies (up to ~5 years), and systematic reviews [1][2][5][7][8][9][10]. A formal risk assessment set an observed safe level of 5 g/day for chronic use [11]; high-dose trials in clinical populations (up to ~10 g/day) reported no significant adverse events [15], including in type 2 diabetics [17].
- **The myth's origin should be explained, not just denied:** (a) supplementation raises *serum creatinine* — a metabolic byproduct — without impairing actual filtration, which can spuriously lower calculated eGFR ("pseudo-renal insufficiency") [1][2][6]; (b) widely cited case reports involved patients with **pre-existing** renal disease [12][13]; (c) 1997 media coverage blamed creatine for three wrestler deaths that the CDC attributed to hyperthermia/dehydration from extreme weight-cutting [14].
- **Required caveat:** Data in established chronic kidney disease are insufficient; one animal model (polycystic kidney disease rats) showed accelerated progression [16], and theoretical concern exists with nephrotoxic drug combinations. Medical supervision is advised in these groups [1][2].

### 5. Dehydration and cramps — **ESTABLISHED as a myth; note its origin honestly**
The claim originated in a 1998 review that was explicitly speculative and anecdote-based [23], plus a 2000 ACSM roundtable *precautionary* statement grounded in theory, not clinical data [22]. Subsequent empirical work refuted it: a systematic review found no impairment of thermoregulation or fluid balance [18]; controlled heat-exercise trials showed no adverse effects [20][21]; and multi-season football data found creatine users had *fewer* cramping, dehydration, and injury episodes [19]. The ISSN position stand states these adverse events "have not been substantiated" [1]. **Nuance to preserve:** the ACSM statement was never formally retracted — it was superseded by evidence — and the only consistent "side effect" is the 1–2 kg mass gain [1].

### 6. Hair loss — **DISPUTED; must not be stated as fact**
This is the claim most in need of revision in typical drafts:
- The entire claim rests on **one 2009 study** of ~20 rugby players that measured *hormones, not hair* [3]. DHT rose ~56% after a loading week but remained **within normal clinical range**; no hair density, shedding, or alopecia outcome was ever measured.
- The finding has **never been replicated**; other creatine trials measuring androgens show no consistent changes [1][2].
- Mechanistic plausibility exists (DHT is genuinely involved in androgenetic alopecia [4]), so the honest formulation is: *"A single small, unreplicated 2009 study observed a transient DHT increase within normal ranges; no study has ever directly measured hair loss as an outcome, and expert reviews conclude the evidence does not support creatine causing baldness [1][2][3]."*

### 7. Cognitive effects — **CONDITIONAL; drafts claiming "creatine boosts brain power" must be qualified**
This is where drafts most commonly overstate the evidence:
- **Null overall:** A 2022 meta-analysis of 25 RCTs found no significant effect on cognition in healthy young adults (g ≈ 0.05, ns) [25].
- **Supported (modest):** Memory improvement in adults ≥65 (g ≈ 0.29–0.32), with little effect on other domains; evidence quality rated low-to-moderate [25][28].
- **Supported (small trials):** Vegetarians/vegans have lower baseline brain creatine and show the clearest response [26][31].
- **Preliminary:** Sleep deprivation — two small RCTs (n≈15–16), including one acute mega-dose (0.35 g/kg) study [29][30]. Clinical applications (TBI, treatment-resistant depression) remain speculative case-series-level evidence [34].
- **Mechanistic caution:** Brain phosphocreatine rises more slowly than muscle (typically requiring ~10 g/day for ≥8 weeks) with substantial individual variability — some individuals show no increase — and cognitive gains do **not** correlate tightly with brain PCr increases [27][32][40].

### 8. Genuine side effects — **ESTABLISHED**
The only well-documented adverse effect is gastrointestinal distress (diarrhea) with large single boluses (≥10 g), mitigated by splitting doses [24]. Third-party-tested products are recommended to avoid contamination [1].

---

## Part 3 — Residual Uncertainties & Verification Gaps (retain in the report)

1. **Recency gap:** The retrieved literature may not capture 2025–2026 publications; replication attempts of the DHT study or the first direct hair-outcome trials could have appeared. Flag as an open verification item.
2. **Effect-size precision:** Figures for the older-adult cognition meta-analysis and the sleep-deprivation trial come from abstracts and may differ slightly from full-text values.
3. **Population limits:** Most cognitive trials are small (n<50), short (≤12 weeks), and conducted in young men; generalization to women, the very old, and long-term use is under-studied [25][27].
4. **Superseded-but-unretracted guidance:** The ACSM 2000 precaution [22] remains formally on record despite being contradicted by later data — worth a footnote, not silence.

---

## References

[1] Kreider RB, et al. ISSN position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine. *J Int Soc Sports Nutr.* 2017;14:18.
[2] Antonio J, et al. Common questions and misconceptions about creatine supplementation. *J Int Soc Sports Nutr.* 2021;18(1):13.
[3] van der Merwe J, Brooks NE, Myburgh KH. Three weeks of creatine monohydrate supplementation affects dihydrotestosterone to testosterone ratio in college-aged rugby players. *Clin J Sport Med.* 2009;19(5):399–404.
[4] Ho CH, Sood T, Zito PM. Androgenetic Alopecia. *StatPearls*, 2024.
[5] Poortmans JR, Francaux M. Long-term oral creatine supplementation does not impair renal function in healthy athletes. *Med Sci Sports Exerc.* 1999;31:1108–1110.
[6] Poortmans JR, Francaux M. Adverse effects of creatine supplementation: fact or fiction? *Sports Med.* 2000;30:155–170.
[7] Robinson TM, et al. *Br J Sports Med.* 2000;34:284–288.
[8] Mayhew DL, et al. *Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab.* 2002;12:283–289.
[9] Kreider RB, et al. *Mol Cell Biochem.* 2003;244:89–94.
[10] Schilling BK, et al. *Med Sci Sports Exerc.* 2001;33:183–188.
[11] Shao A, Hathcock JN. Risk assessment for creatine monohydrate. *Regul Toxicol Pharmacol.* 2006;45:242–251.
[12] Pritchard NR, Kalra PA. *Lancet.* 1998;351:1252–1253.
[13] Koshy KM, et al. *N Engl J Med.* 1999;340:814–815.
[14] CDC. Hyperthermia and dehydration-related deaths in three collegiate wrestlers. *MMWR.* 1998;47:175–182.
[15] Kley RA, et al. Creatine for treating muscle disorders. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev.* 2013;(6):CD004760.
[16] Edmunds JW, et al. *Am J Kidney Dis.* 2001;37:73–78.
[17] Gualano B, et al. *Med Sci Sports Exerc.* 2011;43:770–778.
[18] Lopez RM, et al. Does creatine supplementation hinder exercise heat tolerance or body fluid balance? A systematic review. *J Strength Cond Res.* 2009.
[19] Greenwood M, et al. *Mol Cell Biochem.* 2003.
[20] Watson G, et al. *Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab.* 2004.
[21] Kilduff LP, et al. *Med Sci Sports Exerc.* 2007.
[22] Terjung RL, et al. ACSM roundtable. *Med Sci Sports Exerc.* 2000.
[23] Juhn MS, Tarnopolsky MA. *Clin J Sport Med.* 1998.
[24] Ostojic SM, Ahmetovic Z. *Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab.* 2008.
[25] Forbes SC, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of creatine monohydrate supplementation on cognition. *Nutr Rev.* 2022;80(10):2189–2197.
[26] Rae C, et al. Oral creatine monohydrate supplementation improves brain performance. *Proc R Soc B.* 2003.
[27] Prokopidis K, et al. Creatine supplementation and brain health. *Nutr Rev.* 2023.
[28] Prokopidis K, et al. Creatine supplementation and cognitive function in older adults: systematic review and meta-analysis. *Eur J Nutr.* 2025.
[29] Single high-dose creatine in sleep deprivation (0.35 g/kg, n=15). *Sci Rep.* 2024; s41598-024-54249-9.
[30] McMorris T, et al. *Physiol Behav.* 2006.
[31] Yazigi Solis S, et al. *J Int Soc Sports Nutr.* 2021.
[32] Smith-Ryan AE, et al. Creatine supplementation and brain health. *Exp Gerontol.* 2021.
[34] Avgerinos KI, et al. Creatine augmentation in SSRI-resistant depression. 2018 (PMID 29704837).
[35] Hultman J, et al. Muscle creatine loading in men. *J Appl Physiol.* 1996;81:232–237.
[36] Branch JD. Meta-analysis of creatine and body composition/performance. *Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab.* 2003;13:198–226.
[37] Rawson ES, Volek JS. *J Strength Cond Res.* 2003;17:822–831.
[38] Antonio J, Ciccone V. Pre- vs. post-workout creatine supplementation. *J Int Soc Sports Nutr.* 2013;10:36.
[40] Prokopidis K, Forbes SC, et al. Dose–response review of creatine and brain creatine. *Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr.* 2024.

---

**Summary of revisions:** (1) Hair-loss and kidney/liver-damage claims downgraded from implied fact to "disputed/unsupported, with documented myth origins"; (2) cognitive-enhancement claims restructured from blanket assertions to population-specific tiers (null in rested young adults; modest memory benefit in older adults; preliminary in sleep deprivation); (3) loading-phase necessity corrected to optional; (4) weight-gain characterization corrected from "water bloat" to intracellular water plus lean mass; (5) explicit caveats added for CKD, nephrotoxic drugs, pregnancy/pediatric data gaps, and the 2025–2026 literature recency gap.
